newsitem.title: UAE: FEATURE - After oil, what's next for UAE?
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - After oil, what's next for UAE?

text.p: A generation of United Arab Emirates citizens is dazzled by the vast petrodollars which have turned their backward desert country into a land of plenty.

The Gulf Arab federation, which celebrates its 25th anniversary on December 2, is trying to reduce its vulnerability to the vagaries of world oil markets. It is banking on industrial diversification to guarantee the prosperity to which its people have quickly become accustomed.

"Twenty-five years ago there was nothing here," said Ahmad, 35, as he looked out over Dubai's Jebel Ali Free Zone. Built in 1985 around what officials call the world's biggest man-made port, the zone hosts more than 1,000 companies from 72 countries with investments of about $1.75 billion.
The government hopes it, and another $3 billion zone planned in the capital Abu Dhabi, will provide a platform for expansion in manufacturing and services well into the next century.
"But oil is still the engine for growth. A lot of economic activity still depends on where the oil price is," said Mohamed al-Asoomi, economic research chief at Emirates Industrial Bank.
UAE's oil output of around 2.16 million barrels, most of it from Abu Dhabi, has ensured its 550,000 citizens live in comfort unimaginable 30 years ago.

The welfare state makes possible utility rates amongst the world's cheapest and per capita income near the world's highest -- $29,000 in Abu Dhabi, richest of the seven emirates. Income in Dubai and the other five emirates is lower.
Oil revenue, now $9 billion annually, has lured 1.6 million foreign workers to the tax-free UAE, where skyscrapers tower over deserts once home to rudimentary mud huts.
It has lifted gross domestic product to an estimated 150 billion dirhams ($41 billion) from 40 billion dirhams 20 years ago.
Thanks to the oil earnings, the non-oil sector has been growing too. Asoomi says the sector's contribution to GDP has grown to about 60 percent from around 20 percent 20 years ago.
Like its Gulf neighbours, the UAE wants to reduce reliance on the dominant public sector. But economists say the UAE will find it difficult to wean its people off the welfare system.
"Privatisation is not going to run along Western lines. One route privatised firms take to become more efficient is to cut workforce. This cannot be applied here," said an economist.
"Privatised industry has to charge a full economic rate for services, but that is not going to happen either," he added.

Inflation is an economic bugbear. Officially estimated at five percent, it is independently put at 12 percent due mostly to imported inflation -- a result of the dirham's link to the dollar, the currency in which oil is traded.
This means the economy, which expanded a nominal 6.6 percent in 1995, is shrinking in real terms.
Dependence on cheap foreign labour is another worry. A fast growing local population needs jobs, but not those of labourers.
"It is very hard to forecast the day when UAE will become self-sufficient, even in middle management," a diplomat said.
Despite its success in recent decades, the UAE is missing out on a fundamental ingredient for growth -- a stock exchange.
After years of delayed plans to open one, officials now say that 1997 is the most likely date for a start.

The economies of the seven member emirates are heading along divergent paths. The richest, Abu Dhabi, has oil reserves to support commercial production for at least 100 years, so there is no pressing need to diversify. But experience of mercurial oil prices has taught its leaders to spread risk.
"In future Abu Dhabi will do something to diversify the economy and develop the petrochemicals sector, the oil products industry and industry dependent on energy," Asoomi said.
Once a pearl-trading centre, Dubai has promoted itself as a regional business hub. It recently unveiled an economic plan spelling out life after oil, on which reliance will end by 2010.

It plans to boost high-tech industry, rely more on private business, upgrade labour productivity, encourage capital-intensive production and improve the investment climate. It is also investing heavily in tourism infrastructure.
"Dubai will remain the trade and service centre for the region. There are bureaucratic obstacles, but business adapts and can operate profitably here," a Western diplomat said.
Sharjah has 46 percent of the UAE's industrial concerns and is becoming a centre for manufacturing.
"Sharjah has a good opportunity to develop its gas industry and small- and medium-scale industries because land is cheap and it has gas as a source of energy," Asoomi said.
The smaller and poorer northern emirates will continue to rely on handouts from Abu Dhabi, but Fujairah and Ras al-Khaimah are trying to develop their ports and tourism facilities. ($1=3.67 dirhams)
